newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: EBRD Slovnaft sale may have little impact.
newsitem.headline: EBRD Slovnaft sale may have little impact.

text.p: The proposed sale of the EBRD stake in Slovak oil refiner Slovnaft a.s. may have little effect on foreign confidence in Slovnaft shares despite controversy over the company's privatisation, analysts said on Wednesday.
Much would depend on who the buyer was and what was the price paid for the EBRD (European Bank for Reconstruction and Development) stake, analysts said.

"Everything will depend on the price for the package, and I think the EBRD will decide purely on a commercial basis and will consider the best offer it gets, if there are more of them," said Peter Krutil of Creditanstalt.
Earlier this month the EBRD said it was expecting a proposal from the National Property Fund (NPF), the state privatisation agency, to buy back its stake in Slovnaft.
But like so many deals in the Slovak equity market, the case is far from clear. The NPF responded by saying it had yet to receive a go-ahead from the finance ministry.
Analysts said the NPF would not necessarily be the buyer.
But some analysts said they were not concerned about any effect on foreign sentiment of the planned sale by the EBRD, set up to help post-communist countries build free market economies.

"From the point of view of foreign investors, the move should not have any great effect as they (the buyers) are mostly portfolio investors and not strategic investors like the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development," Dusan Sykora of ING Barings told Reuters.

The EBRD's entry into Slovakia's sole oil refiner was as controversial as its planned exit. It took the stake in 1995 by buying half of Slovnaft's $113 million Global Depositary Receipt (GDR) issue, which flopped on international markets.

The EBRD effectively paid the 1,000 crown face value per share. But shortly afterwards the NPF sold a 39 percent stake in the refiner to a management-led group, Slovintegra, for a price far below the GDR level.
Slovnaft is well-connected politically and the EBRD has expressed general concern about Slovakia's widespread practice of privatising by management buyout.
Analysts predict the NPF will offer part of its stake in Slovnaft to a scheme under which citizens can exchange privatisation bonds for shares from the NPF portfolio.
"If the fund offers Slovnaft shares for exchange for the bonds, then it is important which Slovnaft issue will be offered and for what price," Krutil said.

At present the NPF holds 25 percent of Slovnaft, which was initially privatised in the first wave of mass voucher privatisation completed in 1993. The government last year scrapped the second wave in favour of the privatisation bonds.
Brokers said any plan for the NPF to offer Slovnaft shares from the second issue, made through the GDR programme, would have little success in the bond privatisation scheme.

Second issue Slovnaft shares rarely trade on the Bratislava Stock Exchange. A large parcel of first issue shares sold on Tuesday for 950 crowns each but brokers see the true market rate at around 900.
The NPF recently offered stakes in several minor issues in exchange for the privatisation bonds, but the Slovnaft offer would mark the most prominent firm in the programme so far.

Brokers said there was little demand for Slovnaft shares at the moment. But if the NPF decided to offer them at a low price in exchange for privatisation bonds, this could drag down the market price and might attract more foreign investors.
